source_text: De trinitate 7.1 Ἐκφεύγειν τοιγαροῦν τὸ ἔγκλημα τὸ περὶ τῆς δόξης τῶν κτιστῶν θεῶν τοὺς πιστεύοντας τῷ υἱῷ ὁ ἔννομος Παῦλος τῷ θεϊκῷ πνεύματι σεσοφισμένος ἐγγυᾶται. 7.2 ἔτι δὲ καὶ "ἀθέους" ἀποκαλεῖ τοὺς πρὸ τούτου ἐκτὸς τοῦ υἱοῦ τὸν θεὸν καὶ πατέρα μόνον ἐγνωκότας, ἐπειδὴ οὐκ ἐν π̣ο̣ι̣ήμασι τ̣ελ̣εῖ, γράφων πῇ μὲν ὅτι «μνημονεύετε ὅτι ποτὲ ὑμεῖς τὰ ἔθνη ἐν σαρκί, οἱ λεγόμενοι ἀκροβυστία ὑπὸ τῆς λεγομένης περιτομῆς ἐν σαρκὶ χειροποιήτου, ὅτι ἦτε τῷ καιρῷ ἐκείνῳ χωρὶς Χριστοῦ, ἀπηλλοτρι̣ω̣μ̣ένοι τῆς ἐλπ̣ι´̣δος τοῦ Ἰσραὴλ καὶ ξένοι τῶν διαθηκῶν τῆς ἐπ̣αγγελίας, ἐλπίδα μὴ ἔχοντες καὶ ἄθεοι ἐν τῷ κ̣όσμῳ». 7.3 πῇ δέ «ἀλλὰ τότε μὲν οὐκ εἰδότες θεὸν ἐδουλεύσατε τοῖς φύσει μὴ οὖσι θεοῖς–νῦν δὲ γνόντες θεόν, μᾶλλον γν̣ωσθέντες ὑπὸ θεοῦ, πῶς ἐπιστρέφετε πάλιν ἐπὶ τὰ ἀσθενῆ καὶ πτωχὰ στοιχεῖα, οἷς πάλιν ἄνωθεν δ̣ουλεύειν θ̣έλετε»; 7.4 ἀλλὰ μὴν τοῦ πρεσβυτέρου νόμου τὸ ἀεὶ νέον καὶ οὐκ εἰς γῆρας ἀποκλῖνον σω̣τ̣η´̣ρ̣ιον κήρυγμα τὸ περὶ Χριστοῦ καὶ ἁγίου πνεύματος καὶ τὸν ὡς πάντα τὰ ἄλλα ᾶ παρεὶς ἐκήρυττεν μεγάλα αὐχῶν ὅτι καὶ τὸ δοκοῦν ἐπονείδιστον εἶναι Χριστῷ διὰ τὴν φιλάνθρωπον αὐτοῦ οἰκονομίαν, πᾶσαν εὔκλειαν καὶ ῥώμην βρύει, ἐγᾦμαι τοῦτο ποιῶν ἐξ ἔργου, ἵνα καὶ ἐσταυρωμένον». Ῥωμαίοις δέ· «δικαιοσύνη δὲ θεοῦ διὰ πίστεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ εἰς πάντας τοὺς πιστεύοντας». 7.10 διὰ τῆς εἰς τὸν υἱὸν φησ̣ὶ πίστεως δικαιοῦται ὑπὸ θεοῦ ἕκαστος. 7.11 Γαλάταις δέ· «εἰδότες δὲ ὅτι οὐ δικαιοῦται ἄνθρωπος ἐξ ἔργων νόμου ἐὰν μὴ διὰ πίστεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, καὶ ἡμεῖς εἰς Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐπιστεύσαμεν, ἵνα δικα̣ιωθῶμεν ἐκ πίστεως Χριστοῦ καὶ οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων νόμου, ὅτι ἐξ ἔργων νόμου οὐ δικαιωθήσεται πᾶσα σάρξ». 7.12 ἐξηγεῖται δὲ καὶ ἑτέρωθι ὅτι «οὔτε περιτομή τι ἰσχύει οὔτε ἀκροβυστία, ἀλλὰ καινὴ πίστις δ̣ι̣' α᾿̣γάπης ἐνεργουμένη». 7.13 Τοῦ δὲ λόγου βαθύνοντος τὸν νοῦν ἀναπτυκτέον. 7.14 διδάσκειν μὲν οὖν βούλεται ὡς ἡ Χριστοῦ ἐπιφάνεια καινήν̣ τινα καὶ τὴν μόνην πίστιν ἁ´̣πασιν ἀνθρώποις ἐξεύρετο· καθ' ἣν οὐδεμίαν χώραν οὔτε Ἰουδαισμῷ οὔτε Ἑλληνισμῷ καταλέλοιπεν. 7.15 αὕτη δὲ νοηθ̣ε̣ι´̣η̣ ἂν καὶ κατὰ τό· «ἰδο̣υ`̣ τὰ ἀρχαῖα παρῆλθεν, καινὰ γέγονε̣ν πάν τα». καὶ ἵνα συνελ··ε̣ι̣ παύεται μὲν̣ ὁ τὸν̣ θεὸν εἰδὼς νόμου ὡσ μὴ τελεία̣ν τὴν π̣εριτομὴν φησίν. 7.16 ἀνέλαμψεν δὲ εἰς
pass_a_gloss: 7.1 Therefore the law-abiding Paul, made wise by the divine Spirit, guarantees that those who believe in the Son escape the charge concerning the glory of created gods. 7.2 And further he even calls 'godless' those who before this had known God and Father alone, outside the Son, since he is not counted among things made, writing in one place that 'remember that once you, the nations in flesh, those called foreskin by what is called circumcision in flesh made by hand, that you were at that time without Christ, estranged from the hope of Israel and strangers to the covenants of the promise, not having hope and godless in the world'. 7.3 And in another place: 'but then indeed, not knowing God, you were slaves to those that by nature are not gods; but now, having known God, rather having been known by God, how do you turn back again to the weak and poor elements, to which again from the start you wish to be slaves?' 7.4 But indeed, above the older law he holds the ever new and not declining into old age saving proclamation about Christ and Holy Spirit, and the church ordinance, as more excellent, on account of its being perfect and its having neither anything lawless (damaged) troubling it, nor (damaged) finer or greater must be set before (damaged) in word or in manner (damaged). For in this matter he writes to (damaged, a dative plural ending) on the one hand that 'I became', 'according to zeal persecuting the church, according to righteousness in law having become blameless; but whatever things were gains to me, these I have considered loss because of Christ. But indeed I also consider all things to be loss because of the surpassingness of the knowledge of Jesus Christ our Lord, on account of whom I suffered loss of all things and consider them to be dung, so that I may gain Christ'. 7.5 And on the other hand to Romans: 'for if the one coming preaches another Jesus, whom we did not preach, or you receive another spirit, which you did not receive'. 7.6 Then looking toward what, and thinking what sort of things, has he again written things proper to unmixed knowledge of God? To the Corinthians, the second time, that if anyone is reconciled to the Son, he has been reconciled to God, and that in Christ is the agreement of the world with God. 7.7 And it runs: 'namely that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning to them their trespasses, and having placed in us the word of the reconciliation. So on behalf of Christ we act as envoys, as God exhorting through us. We beg on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God'. 7.8 And again, as though passing over all the other things, he preached, boasting great things, that even what seems to be a reproach to Christ through his man-loving dispensation gushes with all good fame and strength, doing this, I think, on purpose, so that also the one who from the glorious suffering does not discern the uncreated and undefiled and unchangeable Godhead might incur an indictment of arrogance. 7.9 And he said such things: 'I did not judge to know anything among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified'. And to Romans: 'and righteousness of God through faith of Jesus Christ to all those believing'. 7.10 Through the faith toward the Son, he says, each one is justified by God. 7.11 And to Galatians: 'and knowing that a man is not justified from works of law except through faith of Jesus Christ, we too believed into Jesus Christ, so that we might be justified from faith of Christ and not from works of law, because from works of law all flesh will not be justified'. 7.12 And he explains also elsewhere that 'neither circumcision avails anything nor foreskin, but new faith working through love'. 7.13 And as the saying is deep, the sense must be unfolded. 7.14 So he wishes to teach that the appearing of Christ found out a certain new and the only faith for all men, according to which it has left no place either to Judaism or to Hellenism. 7.15 And this might be understood also according to the saying: 'behold, the ancient things passed away, all things have become new'. And so that, to sum up (damaged), the one who knows God ceases on the one hand from law, as he says the circumcision is not perfect. 7.16 But there shone forth for (sentence continues in the next section)
pass_b_english: So Paul, faithful to the law and made wise by the divine Spirit, guarantees that those who believe in the Son escape the charge of giving glory to created gods.

More than that, he even calls “godless” those who before this knew God the Father alone, apart from the Son, since the Son is not counted among the things that were made. In one place he writes: “Remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh, called the uncircumcision by what is called the circumcision, made in the flesh by hand, were at that time without Christ, estranged from the hope of Israel and strangers to the covenants of the promise, having no hope and godless in the world” (Ephesians 2:11-12).

In another: “But then, when you did not know God, you were slaves to beings that by nature are not gods. Now, however, that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and beggarly elements, to which you want to be slaves all over again?” (Galatians 4:8-9).

Yet he holds the saving proclamation about Christ and the Holy Spirit, ever new and never sinking into old age, and the Church’s ordinance, to be more excellent than the older law, because it is perfect and has nothing either [...] lawless [...] to trouble it, or [...] finer or greater that ought to be set before it [...] in word or in manner [...]. For on this matter he writes to [...]: “I became”; “as to zeal, a persecutor of the church; as to the righteousness that is in the law, blameless. But whatever gains I had, these I have counted loss for Christ’s sake. Indeed, I count all things to be loss because of the surpassing excellence of the knowledge of Jesus Christ our Lord, for whose sake I have suffered the loss of all things and count them as refuse, that I may gain Christ” (Philippians 3:6-8).
And to the Romans: “For if the one who comes preaches another Jesus, whom we did not preach, or if you receive a different spirit, which you did not receive” (2 Corinthians 11:4).

With what in view, then, and with what thoughts proper to a pure knowledge of God, has he written again? To the Corinthians, in the second letter, that if anyone is reconciled to the Son, he has been reconciled to God, and that the world’s accord with God is in Christ. The passage runs: “That God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and placing in us the word of reconciliation. So we are ambassadors on behalf of Christ, as though God were appealing through us. We plead on Christ’s behalf: be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:19-20).

And again, as though he had set everything else aside, he proclaimed with great boasting that even what seems to bring reproach on Christ, because of his loving dispensation for mankind, teems with all honour and strength. He does this, I think, on purpose, so that anyone who does not discern, from the glorious passion, the uncreated, pure and unchangeable Godhead may stand indicted for arrogance.

His words were these: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2). And to the Romans: “The righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe” (Romans 3:22). Through faith in the Son, he says, each person is justified by God.

And to the Galatians: “Knowing that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, we too have believed in Jesus Christ, so that we might be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law; for by works of the law no flesh will be justified” (Galatians 2:16). And elsewhere too he explains that “neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but a new faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6).

The saying runs deep, and its sense must be unfolded. What he means to teach is that the appearing of Christ found a new faith, the only faith, for all people, and by it left no room either for Judaism or for the religion of the Greeks. This faith may also be understood by the saying: “See, the old things have passed away; all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17). And, to put it briefly [...], the one who knows God ceases from the law, since, he says, circumcision is not perfect. But there shone forth for …

choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. Wrong clauses fixed: 7.1 ‘the Paul of the Law’; 7.2 ἐπειδὴ οὐκ ἐν ποιήμασι τελεῖ (the Son is not counted among things made) had become ‘their knowledge does not come to completion in works’; 7.4 τοῦ πρεσβυτέρου νόμου is a genitive of comparison (the new proclamation is more excellent than the older law), the draft made it ‘the ecclesiastical order of the elder Law’ and filled the damaged lines with invented sense; 7.6 Ἆρα … question lost and σύμβασις made ‘covenant’; 7.8 the indictment of the one who ‘does not discern’ the Godhead inverted into ‘does not look down upon’; 7.13-7.15 garbled; 7.16 ἀνέλαμψεν rendered ‘took up into’. References: nine abbreviated forms written out; Ephesians 2:12 widened to 2:11-12 (the quotation starts at verse 11); 2 Corinthians 5:19 widened to 5:19-20; 2 Corinthians 11:4 added to the quotation Didymus introduces as ‘to the Romans’. No edition numbers in the reading text.

choices.why: ἔννομος echoes Paul’s own ἔννομος Χριστοῦ (1 Corinthians 9:21); ‘the Paul of the Law’ is not English and misleads.

choices.term: τὸ ἔγκλημα τὸ περὶ τῆς δόξης τῶν κτιστῶν θεῶν
choices.english: the charge of giving glory to created gods
choices.why: The charge is idolatry, worshipping creatures; believing in a Son who is not a creature clears it.

choices.english: since the Son is not counted among the things that were made
choices.why: τελεῖν ἐν = be ranked among; subject is the Son. Knowing the Father without the Son is ‘godless’ because the Son is God, not a creature.

Lacunae and broken words in the copy-text (ἀνομ…, ··κάλλιον, προτεθη ο··, καλλ…, π̣ε̣π…σι, συνελ··ε̣ι̣). Legible words translated; gaps marked. ‘to put it briefly’ reads συνελ··ει as συνελὼν εἰπεῖν (conjecture, see problems).
Didymus quotes the single word before Philippians 3:6; kept as a separate quotation, not merged into the verse.
The words are 2 Corinthians 11:4; Didymus (or his copy) names Romans. His wording kept, the real verse cited.
Didymus’ text of Galatians 5:6 reads ‘new faith’ (cf. καινὴ κτίσις, Galatians 6:15); his wording kept, and 7.14 builds on it.
With the following purpose clause (ἵνα) the phrase marks deliberate intent.
Paired with Judaism as a religion; ‘Hellenism’ alone suggests culture.
The sentence runs on into the next section (σωτηρίαν … ὁ υἱός); only the words this section holds are translated.
